title: What If My Jaw Hurts When I Wear Whitening Trays?
excerpt: Experiencing jaw pain when wearing whitening trays? Learn the common causes, what the symptoms may indicate, and when to seek professional dental advice.
author: Teeth Whitening Team
imageAlt: What If My Jaw Hurts When I Wear Whitening Trays?
body:
Introduction

Teeth whitening is one of the most popular cosmetic dental treatments in the UK, and custom-fitted whitening trays are a widely used method for achieving a brighter smile at home. However, some people find that wearing whitening trays causes unexpected jaw discomfort — a concern that often prompts a search online before a visit to the dentist.

If you have experienced jaw pain when wearing whitening trays, you are not alone. This symptom can arise for several reasons, ranging from how the trays fit in the mouth to underlying jaw joint sensitivities that may not have been previously noticed. Understanding what might be causing the discomfort can help you make more informed decisions about your treatment and oral health.

This article explores the common reasons jaw pain can occur during tray-based teeth whitening, what the underlying dental science suggests, practical steps you can take to manage discomfort, and when it may be appropriate to seek a professional dental assessment. As with any dental symptom, individual circumstances vary, and a qualified dentist is best placed to offer personalised guidance.

Why does my jaw hurt when wearing whitening trays?

Jaw pain when wearing whitening trays is most commonly caused by ill-fitting trays placing prolonged pressure on the teeth and jaw joints, or by clenching the jaw during wear. It may also aggravate an existing temporomandibular joint (TMJ) condition. This symptom warrants a professional dental review to identify the cause and determine whether whitening treatment is suitable for you.

Common Reasons for Jaw Pain During Teeth Whitening

Jaw pain during tray-based whitening is not an expected part of the treatment, but it is a recognised concern that patients occasionally raise with their dentists. Several factors may contribute to this discomfort.

Ill-Fitting Whitening Trays

One of the most frequent causes is trays that do not fit correctly. Over-the-counter whitening kits often include generic trays that are not made to match the precise shape of your teeth and jaws. When a tray is too tight, too loose, or poorly contoured, it can place uneven pressure on the teeth, gums, and surrounding jaw structures during the period of wear.

Custom-fitted trays provided by a dental professional are made from impressions or digital scans of your own teeth. This means they are designed to sit closely against each tooth surface, reducing the risk of unnecessary jaw strain. If you are experiencing jaw pain with a non-custom tray, this may be a contributing factor worth discussing with your dentist.

Unconscious Jaw Clenching

Some people find that wearing something in their mouth — whether a dental tray, a sports guard, or a retainer — causes them to clench their jaw muscles without realising it. This is particularly common during periods of focus, stress, or sleep.

Sustained jaw clenching places significant strain on the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), the muscles of mastication (chewing muscles), and the surrounding soft tissues. Even a short period of clenching each day during whitening wear time can result in jaw soreness or a dull ache that persists after the trays have been removed.

Understanding the Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) and Whitening

The temporomandibular joint connects the lower jaw (mandible) to the skull at a point just in front of each ear. It is one of the most complex joints in the body, responsible for the movements involved in chewing, speaking, and swallowing.

TMJ disorders — often grouped under the term temporomandibular dysfunction (TMD) — are relatively common and can cause jaw pain, clicking or popping sounds, limited mouth opening, and headaches. Many people live with mild TMD without a formal diagnosis, simply managing the discomfort as part of daily life.

If you have an underlying susceptibility to TMJ-related discomfort, wearing whitening trays may bring this to the surface. The trays alter the resting position of the jaw slightly, which can place additional load on a joint that is already working under strain. For individuals with pre-existing TMD, even short periods of tray wear may trigger or worsen jaw pain.

It is worth noting that this does not mean teeth whitening is unsuitable for everyone with jaw sensitivity — but it does mean that a clinical assessment beforehand is particularly valuable. A dentist can assess jaw joint health and advise on whether whitening with trays is appropriate, and if so, what modifications may help. For a deeper look at this scenario, see can you use whitening trays if you have TMJ pain.

If you are considering a professional whitening treatment and have jaw concerns, you may find it helpful to review the teeth whitening cost and treatment options to understand what professionally supervised care involves.

How Tray Design Affects Jaw Comfort

The physical design of a whitening tray plays a more significant role in jaw comfort than many patients might expect.

Tray Thickness and Material

Thicker trays, often found in cheaper over-the-counter products, can raise the bite slightly. When the upper and lower teeth cannot close naturally, the jaw muscles must work harder to accommodate the altered bite position. This muscular effort, sustained over the recommended wear period — sometimes one to two hours or more — can lead to jaw fatigue and discomfort.

Professionally made trays are generally thinner, flexible, and precisely contoured to minimise bite alteration and avoid unnecessary pressure on the gums and teeth.

Tray Length and Coverage

Trays that extend too far back towards the molars or that have excess material around the gum line may cause awkward positioning of the lower jaw during wear. This can create tension in the jaw muscles and the TMJ region over time.

A dental professional fitting custom trays will trim and adjust them to ensure they sit comfortably without interfering with natural jaw alignment.

The Relationship Between Tooth Sensitivity and Jaw Pain

It is also worth understanding that not all discomfort associated with whitening trays originates in the jaw itself. Tooth sensitivity is a well-documented side effect of peroxide-based whitening treatments. The active whitening agent temporarily increases the permeability of dental enamel, which can cause a sharp or aching sensation in the teeth.

Referred dental pain — where discomfort originating in the teeth is perceived in the jaw, temples, or ear area — can sometimes be mistaken for jaw joint pain. This is because the nerves supplying the teeth and jaw are closely related, and localising dental pain can sometimes be difficult without a professional examination.

If the sensation you are experiencing feels like a deep ache in the jaw rather than sharp tooth sensitivity, or if it persists for several hours after tray removal, this may suggest a different underlying cause that warrants dental review.

You can learn more about how sensitivity relates to the whitening process by discussing whitening sensitivity in detail with your dental professional during your review.

Practical Steps to Reduce Jaw Discomfort During Whitening

If you are currently experiencing mild jaw discomfort when wearing whitening trays, there are some practical measures that may help, though these should not replace professional advice. If tray tolerance is an issue generally, this article on wearing whitening trays without gagging can also be useful.

Reduce Wear Time Temporarily

If your dentist has prescribed a specific wear duration, it is worth contacting them to discuss whether this can be adjusted. Reducing wear time per session — for example, from two hours to forty-five minutes — may allow you to continue treatment while your jaw acclimatises, or while an underlying issue is assessed.

Avoid Wearing Trays at Night

If you have been using your whitening trays overnight, switching to daytime wear may help. Night-time use can increase the risk of unconscious clenching and grinding (bruxism), which is associated with elevated jaw muscle tension during sleep.

Apply Warm Compresses

A warm flannel or heat pack applied gently to the jaw area after tray removal may help relax the muscles and reduce soreness. If gum irritation is also present, see this guide on sore gums after whitening trays. This is a supportive measure and not a treatment for any underlying condition.

Maintain a Soft Diet on Whitening Days

On days when you notice more jaw sensitivity, choosing softer foods that require less chewing effort can help reduce additional strain on the TMJ and surrounding muscles.

Inform Your Dental Professional

If you are undergoing professionally supervised whitening, always let your dentist know about any jaw discomfort you experience. They can review the fit of your trays, assess your jaw joint health, and advise whether any changes to your treatment plan are appropriate.

When to Seek a Professional Dental Assessment

While mild, temporary jaw discomfort may resolve on its own, there are situations where seeking a dental assessment sooner rather than later is advisable.

You should consider contacting your dentist if you notice any of the following:

  • Jaw pain that persists for more than a day or two after wearing your trays
  • A clicking, popping, or grating sensation in the jaw joint during or after tray use
  • Difficulty opening or closing your mouth comfortably
  • Pain radiating from the jaw into the ear, temple, or neck area
  • Swelling around the jaw or face at any time
  • Jaw pain that is worsening over successive whitening sessions rather than remaining stable or improving

These symptoms do not necessarily indicate a serious problem, but they do suggest that a clinical assessment is appropriate before continuing whitening treatment. A dentist can examine the fit of your trays, assess the jaw joint and surrounding muscles, and identify whether any underlying condition such as TMD may need attention alongside or before your whitening treatment continues.

It is also worth noting that if you have not yet begun whitening treatment and you already experience jaw pain, clicking, or difficulty with jaw movement, mentioning these symptoms at your whitening consultation will allow your dentist to factor them into their recommendations.

For those exploring professional dental whitening for the first time, contact our team to arrange a suitable consultation before committing to a treatment plan.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice

Taking a few preventative steps before and during whitening treatment can reduce the likelihood of experiencing jaw discomfort.

Choose Professionally Supervised Whitening

Opting for whitening treatment overseen by a registered dental professional means your trays will be custom-made from accurate impressions of your teeth. This reduces the risk of tray-related pressure or bite interference. In the UK, teeth whitening using bleaching agents above a certain concentration is a reserved dental treatment and can only legally be prescribed and supervised by a registered dental professional.

Disclose Any History of Jaw Problems

Before starting any whitening treatment, inform your dentist about any history of jaw pain, jaw clicking, headaches linked to the jaw, or previous TMJ-related treatment. This background information allows your clinician to make a more informed assessment of treatment suitability.

Maintain Good Stress Management

Stress is a significant contributing factor to both teeth grinding (bruxism) and jaw clenching. Practices that support stress management — such as regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and mindfulness techniques — may indirectly reduce jaw tension during tray use.

Attend Regular Dental Check-Ups

Routine dental examinations allow your dentist to monitor the health of your teeth, gums, and jaw over time. Any early signs of TMJ changes or bruxism can be identified and managed before they become more significant concerns.

Key Points to Remember

  • Jaw pain when wearing whitening trays is not a normal expected outcome and should be taken seriously.
  • Ill-fitting trays are a common contributing cause, particularly with over-the-counter products that use generic sizing.
  • Unconscious jaw clenching during tray wear can place strain on the TMJ and surrounding muscles.
  • Individuals with existing TMJ sensitivity or TMD may be more susceptible to jaw discomfort during whitening treatment.
  • Tooth sensitivity pain can sometimes be perceived as jaw pain due to referred sensation — professional assessment can help distinguish between the two.
  • Persistent jaw pain, clicking, swelling, or worsening discomfort should prompt a dental review before continuing treatment.
  • Professionally supervised whitening with custom-fitted trays may reduce the risk of jaw discomfort compared to generic over-the-counter alternatives, as the trays are made to fit your individual dentition.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal to have jaw pain after wearing whitening trays?

Mild jaw tiredness after an extended period of wearing trays is not unheard of, particularly if you are new to tray use. However, genuine jaw pain — especially pain that persists beyond a few hours after removing the trays, or that worsens over time — is not a typical or expected outcome of teeth whitening treatment. If you are experiencing jaw pain regularly during whitening, this is worth raising with your dentist so the cause can be identified and your treatment plan reviewed if necessary.

Can teeth whitening trays make TMJ worse?

For some individuals with pre-existing temporomandibular dysfunction (TMD), wearing whitening trays may aggravate jaw joint discomfort. This is because the trays can slightly alter the resting position of the jaw, increasing pressure on an already sensitive joint. If you have a history of TMJ problems, it is important to discuss this with your dentist before starting whitening treatment. They can assess whether adjustments to tray design, wear time, or timing of treatment are appropriate for your situation.

Why do my jaw muscles ache after using whitening trays overnight?

Wearing whitening trays overnight can increase the risk of jaw muscle aching for two main reasons. First, during sleep many people unconsciously clench or grind their teeth, and having a tray in place can amplify this muscular activity. Second, sustained jaw posture over several hours places continuous low-level strain on the temporomandibular joint and surrounding muscles. If overnight use is causing jaw aches, your dentist may recommend switching to shorter daytime sessions, or assess whether a different tray design would be more comfortable for you.

Should I stop using whitening trays if my jaw hurts?

If you are experiencing noticeable jaw pain during or after whitening tray use, it is sensible to pause treatment and contact your dental professional for advice. Continuing to use trays whilst jaw pain is present without understanding the cause may risk aggravating an underlying condition. Your dentist can assess whether the trays need adjustment, whether there is a jaw-related issue that warrants attention, and whether and when it is appropriate to resume whitening treatment.

Can the whitening gel itself cause jaw pain?

The whitening gel used in tray-based treatments — typically a hydrogen or carbamide peroxide formulation — is not generally a direct cause of jaw pain. However, the gel can cause increased tooth sensitivity, which may occasionally be perceived as a broader aching sensation in the jaw area due to referred dental pain. If the discomfort you feel is more of a sharp or tingling sensitivity in the teeth themselves rather than a deep muscular or joint ache, this is more likely sensitivity-related. Your dentist can help determine the origin of your discomfort during an examination.

Are some people more likely to experience jaw pain with whitening trays?

Yes, certain individuals may be more susceptible. People with a history of TMJ disorders, bruxism (teeth grinding), stress-related jaw clenching, or those with naturally narrow arches may find tray-based whitening more uncomfortable. Additionally, anyone using generic over-the-counter trays rather than custom-fitted professional trays has a higher risk of tray-related jaw strain. Disclosing your full dental and medical history to your dentist before starting whitening treatment allows them to tailor their recommendations to your individual circumstances.

Conclusion

Jaw pain when wearing whitening trays is a symptom that deserves attention rather than being dismissed as a minor inconvenience. Understanding that this discomfort can arise from tray fit, unconscious clenching, TMJ sensitivity, or referred dental pain empowers you to take informed steps — whether that means pausing treatment, adjusting your wear routine, or seeking professional dental advice.

Teeth whitening under professional supervision, using custom-fitted trays designed to match your individual anatomy, is a clinically recommended approach for adults considering this treatment in the UK. If you are experiencing jaw pain when wearing whitening trays, speaking with a qualified dental professional is the most reliable way to identify the cause and determine the most suitable path forward.
